model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about my oldest friend. She is a girl who was living next door to my family. We know each other since we are six years old, so it is a very long time.

When we were children we played together every day. We ride our bicycles in the street and we went to the same primary school. After that we go to different secondary schools, but we still met in the weekends, so we never stopped being friends.

Now she is living in another city because of her work. So we don't meet very often, maybe two times in a year. But we send voice messages and sometimes they are very long. And in the summer she comes back and we do something together. Last year we went to the coast for three days and it was very nice.

I think our friendship is lasting because she is a very nice person. She is also very easy, I don't need to explain myself with her. And she knows my family also, my mother likes her very much, so it is comfortable. So this is my oldest friend and why we are still friends until now.

what_caps_it.point: Five sentences begin with 'so'; the answer reads as a list of facts, not a portrait.
The tense slides between past and present four times inside one short story.
'Nice', 'easy', 'comfortable' — the whole characterisation runs on three flat adjectives.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The friend I want to talk about is somebody I've known longer than anyone outside my family — we've been friends since we were six, so that's more than twenty years now.

She grew up in the house next door, which is the whole reason we met. There was nothing chosen about it: our parents put us on the same street, we got on, and by the time we were about eight we were more or less inseparable. We went to different secondary schools, and I remember being genuinely worried that we'd drift apart, but somehow it never happened. We simply went back to the same street every afternoon, and that was that.

These days it's a lot more low-key. She moved away for work about six years ago, so we're down to voice notes — long, rambling ones, usually recorded while one of us is walking somewhere — plus one proper trip a year. It sounds thin written down, but it has turned out to be plenty. Last summer we spent three days on the coast and barely did anything, which was the point.

As for why it's lasted, I have actually thought about this. It isn't that we have a huge amount in common; honestly, we don't. It's that she knew me before I had any image to protect, so there's nothing to perform. And neither of us keeps score — if six months go by, nobody's counting. There's a version of this where the two of us would have let it fade quietly, and I'm well aware of that. What you can't manufacture is a shared history, and that's really all it comes down to.

what_lifts_it.point: 'We've been friends since' fixes the duration, and the narrative then stays reliably in the past.
'Drift apart', 'low-key', 'keeps score' — chunks and precise phrases replace 'nice' and 'easy'.
Three signposted moves, and a close that generalises instead of restating the card.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The person I'd pick is the friend I've had longest — we've been in each other's lives since we were six, which is going on twenty-five years.

It was pure accident. She lived in the house next door, our parents were friendly, and we were simply handed to each other the way the children of neighbours are. What I find interesting, looking back, is that we've never had a great deal in common. Different subjects, different politics, different taste in almost everything. Had we met at twenty rather than at six, I doubt we'd have got past a polite conversation. The friendship predates every opinion either of us currently holds.

She moved away for work some years ago, so the shape of it has changed. It runs on voice notes now — the sort you record while walking, twelve minutes long and about nothing — plus one trip a year where we deliberately do as little as possible. The frequency has dropped and the weight of it hasn't, which I genuinely had not expected.

As to why it's survived, I think it comes down to her having known me before I'd built anything to defend. There's no version of me she hasn't already watched fail, which is oddly restful. Neither of us keeps a ledger, either; six months of silence isn't held against anybody. And that, I suspect, is what people actually mean by an old friend — not somebody you see often, but somebody in front of whom you don't have to be anyone in particular.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion — 'Had we met…' — replaces the standard conditional band 7 never reaches for.
'Handed to each other', 'keeps a ledger', 'oddly restful' — precise rather than decorative.
Closes on a definition of old friendship, not on this particular friendship.

annotations.why: One well-placed image beats five ornamental idioms.

annotations.span: twelve minutes long and about nothing

annotations.why: Group short items into a single run and fall on the last one.

annotations.why: Abstracting in the final sentence lifts the whole turn out of anecdote.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to tell about a person who helped me when I had a difficult time. She was a student in the year above me at my college.

The problem was that my father was in the hospital for six weeks and I stopped going to my classes. So I was behind of all my work. I had three essays and I don't do any of them. I am very stressed at that time and I don't tell anybody about it, not even my friends.

Then one day she sends me a message. She is asking me why I am not coming to the Thursday class. I said I have some problems at home. And then she said we can go to the library on Sunday morning and do the work together. So we did that for six weeks. She made a list every week and we do one thing every time.

In the end I finished all the essays and I passed the year. I felt very grateful because she didn't have to do this, we were not even close friends before. She was very kind and very helpful. So this is the person who helped me when I was struggling.

what_caps_it.point: Past and present alternate all the way through, and reported speech never shifts back.
The turn is a chain of events with no evaluation until the last four words.
'Kind', 'helpful' and 'grateful' are the only evaluative words in the whole answer.

annotations.span: She was a student in the year above me at my college.
annotations.label: Places the person immediately
annotations.why: Locating somebody early stops you explaining who they are twice.

annotations.span: I had three essays and I don't do any of them.
annotations.label: Present tense inside a past story
annotations.why: Choose past simple in sentence one and refuse to leave it.

annotations.span: She is asking me why I am not coming to the Thursday class.
annotations.label: Reported speech doesn't shift back
annotations.why: Say 'She asked me why I wasn't coming' — the whole clause moves back.

annotations.span: I was behind of all my work
annotations.label: Wrong preposition in a fixed phrase
annotations.why: It is 'behind with your work'. Learn the preposition inside the chunk.

annotations.span: She was very kind and very helpful.
annotations.label: Two flat adjectives, no behaviour
annotations.why: Say what she did instead: 'she never once asked what had happened'.

annotations.span: So this is the person who helped me when I was struggling.
annotations.label: Ends by reading the card back
annotations.why: Finish on what the episode taught you about accepting help.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The person I'd like to talk about is somebody I barely knew at the time, which is partly why it stuck with me. She was a year above me on the same course.

This was during my second year. My father was in hospital for about six weeks, and although it all resolved perfectly well in the end, I more or less stopped functioning while it was going on. I carried on turning up to my job and simply stopped going in to college, and by the time I looked up properly I had three essays outstanding and no idea where to start. I hadn't told a single person either, which made the whole thing considerably worse.

What she did was very small. She sent me a message out of the blue asking why I hadn't been at the Thursday seminar, and when I gave her a vague answer she suggested we meet in the library on Sunday morning. We ended up doing that for six weeks. She'd write a list at the start of each session, we'd get through one thing, and then she'd go off and do her own work.

The part I keep coming back to is that she never once asked me what had happened. She treated the whole thing as admin rather than as a crisis, and that was exactly what I needed, because at that point I couldn't have talked about it anyway. If she'd made a big deal of it, I think I'd have avoided her completely. The useful sort of help, it turns out, is rarely the dramatic sort.

what_lifts_it.point: A past perfect and a third conditional break up the flat run of past simples.
'Out of the blue', 'stopped functioning' and 'made a big deal of it' carry the evaluation.
Every paragraph opens with a signpost, so the listener always knows which bullet is running.

annotations.span: The person I'd like to talk about is somebody I barely knew at the time
annotations.label: Names the person and the angle at once
annotations.why: Saying why she is interesting stops the turn becoming a list of facts.

annotations.span: by the time I looked up properly I had three essays outstanding
annotations.label: Time clause layers two moments
annotations.why: 'By the time' lets you skip weeks without losing the listener.

annotations.span: What she did was very small.
annotations.label: Previews the next chunk in five words
annotations.why: A short framing sentence buys thinking time and sounds deliberate.

annotations.span: out of the blue
annotations.label: A chunk retrieved whole
annotations.why: Reuse it for anything unexpected: a message, an offer, a visit.

annotations.span: The part I keep coming back to is that
annotations.label: Signposts the evaluation bullet
annotations.why: Say it aloud and you cannot forget the bullet that carries the band.

annotations.span: she never once asked me what had happened
annotations.label: Stress lands on 'once'
annotations.why: Contrastive stress makes the point without adding a single word.

annotations.span: She treated the whole thing as admin rather than as a crisis
annotations.label: A precise contrast instead of an adjective
annotations.why: Naming what something was not is a cheap way to be exact.

annotations.span: If she'd made a big deal of it, I think I'd have avoided her completely.
annotations.label: Third conditional in its natural home
annotations.why: 'How did it feel' bullets almost always want an unreal past.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The person I want to describe was, at the time, not far off a stranger. She was a year ahead of me on the same course and we had probably exchanged four sentences in total.

The context is quickly told. My father spent six weeks in hospital during my second year, and although it resolved perfectly well, I quietly went to pieces. I kept turning up to my job and stopped turning up to anything else, and by the point I raised my head I was three essays down with no obvious route back. Nor had I told a soul, which is the part that compounds it.

Her intervention was almost aggressively undramatic. A message arrived asking where I'd got to on Thursday; I gave her a non-answer; she proposed the library, Sunday, nine o'clock. That ran for six weeks. She'd draw up a list, we'd knock off one item, and then she'd get on with her own work and leave me to it.

What has stayed with me is the thing she didn't do. Not once did she ask what had gone wrong. She dealt with it as a scheduling problem rather than an emotional one, which was the only version of help I was capable of accepting. Had she sat me down for a heart-to-heart, I'd have found reasons to be busy for the rest of term. I suspect that generalises: the help that works is rarely the help that looks like helping.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Nor had I' and 'Not once did she' put two inversions where band 7 used plain order.
'Went to pieces', 'knock off one item' and 'a heart-to-heart' sit naturally, not on display.
The close generalises the lesson instead of restating what the person did.

annotations.span: Nor had I told a soul
annotations.label: 'Nor' plus inversion joins two negatives
annotations.why: One of the cheapest ways to sound controlled inside a narrative.

annotations.span: Not once did she ask what had gone wrong.
annotations.label: Negative fronting for emphasis
annotations.why: Put the negative first and invert; it still sounds spoken, not written.

annotations.span: almost aggressively undramatic
annotations.label: An unexpected pairing that is exactly right
annotations.why: Precision at this level comes from the adverb, not from rare nouns.

annotations.span: I quietly went to pieces
annotations.label: Idiom placed where a native would
annotations.why: Two natural idioms in two minutes beat five decorative ones.

annotations.span: she proposed the library, Sunday, nine o'clock
annotations.label: Three items on one falling run
annotations.why: Keep the list level in pitch, then drop on the final item.

annotations.span: the help that works is rarely the help that looks like helping
annotations.label: Ends on a generalisation
annotations.why: Lifting out of the anecdote in the last clause raises the whole turn.

cue_card.topic: Describe somebody you know who makes you laugh.
bullets: who this person is
when you usually see them
the kind of thing they say or do
and explain why you think they have that effect on people.
rounding_off: Do other people find them as funny as you do?
Are you funny in the same way yourself?

teaching.band_move: Show the humour, don't label it. One retold episode beats five sentences saying he's funny.

prep_plan.idea_prompt: Choose whoever you can quote. If you can't reproduce one thing they actually said, pick somebody else within five seconds.
prep_plan.trap: Nobody can describe funny. Without one specific retold moment this card produces ninety seconds of adjectives.

time_plan.goal: Name the person and the surprising thing about them.
Who they are and when you actually see them.
One episode, retold with three concrete details.
What their humour does to the people around them.
One line on what funny people are for.

recovery_moves.prompt: Zoom in on the delivery: the face, the pace, whether the voice ever changes.
Bring in a listener: say which relative laughs hardest and which one doesn't.
Contrast them with somebody who tells actual jokes and gets nothing.
Say out loud whether you'd want to be funny in that way yourself.

error_watchlist.wrong: He never tell jokes, he just describe things that happened.
error_watchlist.right: He never tells jokes, he just describes things that happened.
error_watchlist.why: Present habits take -s after he, she or it.

error_watchlist.wrong: It was very funny for me and I felt very fun.
error_watchlist.right: It was hilarious, and I found the whole thing very funny.
error_watchlist.why: 'Fun' is a noun; the adjective you want is 'funny'.

error_watchlist.wrong: So he starts to describe the queue and everybody was laughing.
error_watchlist.right: So he started describing the queue and everybody was laughing.
error_watchlist.why: An episode told in the past stays in the past.

pronunciation_focus.why_here: Deadpan humour lives entirely in delivery; said on one flat pitch, the best line dies.

target_words.note: Stress the second syllable and let the pitch fall.
Two level syllables; the flatness is the joke.
Stress the second; reduce everything after it.
Stress the first syllable; keep the /t/ crisp.
Stress the third syllable, never the first.

chunking_drill.sentence: It was funny because he refused to let any of it go.
chunks: to let any of it go.

minimal_pairs.contrast: rising for disbelief, falling for a plain statement

teaching.examiner_note: You will not get a laugh. The examiner stays neutral by training, and reading their face for a reaction only damages your own delivery.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a person who makes me laugh. He is my uncle, he is the youngest brother of my mother, and he is around fifty years old.

He is coming to our house almost every month for lunch. He is a very funny person but he never tell jokes. He just describes normal things. For example one time he was talking about the post office in his town. He was waiting there for twenty minutes and he described everything, the old man in front of him, the woman with the small dog, the machine that was not working. He was talking maybe twenty minutes and everybody was laughing so much.

And the thing is, his face is always serious. He doesn't laugh himself. So this makes it more funny for us.

I like him because when he is there, nobody is arguing. In my family sometimes people argue at lunch about politics and other things. But when my uncle starts to talk, everybody just listen and laugh. Even my cousins who are very shy, they talk more. So he is a very good person to have in the family and this is why he makes me laugh.

what_caps_it.point: Third-person -s disappears repeatedly, and a continuous form is used for a monthly habit.
'Funny', 'good' and 'serious' carry every judgement in the whole turn.
'So' and 'and' link nearly every idea, and the close repeats the prompt.

annotations.span: For example one time he was talking about the post office in his town.
annotations.label: Moves to a concrete example
annotations.why: Keep this. One retold example is worth more than five adjectives.

annotations.span: He is coming to our house almost every month for lunch.
annotations.label: Continuous used for a habit
annotations.why: Repeated events take the present simple: 'He comes to our house every month.'

annotations.span: he never tell jokes
annotations.label: Third-person -s dropped
annotations.why: Habits with he or she always take -s: 'he never tells jokes'.

annotations.span: So this makes it more funny for us.
annotations.label: Wrong comparative form
annotations.why: Say 'funnier'. Two-syllable adjectives in -y take -er, not 'more'.

annotations.span: So he is a very good person to have in the family and this is why he makes me laugh.
annotations.label: Closes by restating the card
annotations.why: Close on what humour does to a room instead of on the prompt.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The person who makes me laugh most is my mother's youngest brother, so my uncle. He's in his early fifties and he's been coming to our family lunches for as long as I can remember.

What's odd is that he doesn't tell jokes at all. I don't think I've ever heard him tell one. What he does instead is describe something completely ordinary in far too much detail. The one everybody in my family still quotes is his account of queuing in a post office. He'd been waiting about twenty minutes, and he took roughly the same amount of time to describe it: the man in front of him who kept counting his change, the woman with a dog in a bag, the ticket machine that had been broken since the previous winter. None of it was funny in itself. It was funny because he refused to let any of it go.

The other half of it is the delivery. He keeps a completely straight face throughout. He's never once laughed at his own story, which somehow makes everybody else laugh harder.

As for why I like it so much, it really isn't about the jokes. My family argues at the table, mostly about things nobody's going to resolve, and the moment he starts one of these accounts the whole argument simply stops. Even the cousins who barely speak end up joining in. That's the useful thing about somebody funny: they change the temperature of a room and nobody notices them doing it.

what_lifts_it.point: A past perfect and two relative clauses replace the band-6 chain of simple sentences.
'Keeps a straight face', 'refused to let it go', 'change the temperature of a room'.
The example is set up, delivered and then explained, so the humour has a visible shape.

annotations.span: What's odd is that he doesn't tell jokes at all.
annotations.label: Opens on the surprising thing
annotations.why: Leading with what is unexpected gives a listener a reason to keep listening.

annotations.span: the ticket machine that had been broken since the previous winter
annotations.label: Past perfect inside a relative clause
annotations.why: One layered clause shows range without lengthening the sentence.

annotations.span: He keeps a completely straight face throughout.
annotations.label: A collocation, not a description
annotations.why: 'Keep a straight face' is the phrase; assembling it word by word costs marks.

annotations.span: The other half of it is the delivery.
annotations.label: Announces the second part
annotations.why: Numbering your parts aloud makes a turn sound planned rather than remembered.

annotations.span: As for why I like it so much
annotations.label: Signposts the explain bullet
annotations.why: Name the move and you cannot skip the bullet that carries the band.

annotations.span: It was funny because he refused to let any of it go.
annotations.label: Explains the humour precisely
annotations.why: Say what the person does and 'funny' stops having to do all the work.

annotations.span: which somehow makes everybody else laugh harder
annotations.label: Non-defining relative adds a result
annotations.why: A comma plus 'which' adds a consequence without starting a new sentence.

annotations.span: None of it was funny in itself.
annotations.label: Falls hard on 'itself'
annotations.why: The contrast is carried by stress here, not by extra words.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The funniest person I know is my mother's youngest brother, and the peculiar thing about him is that he has never, to my knowledge, told a joke.

What he does is narrate. He takes some event of no consequence whatsoever and refuses to abbreviate it. The one my family has more or less canonised is his account of a post office queue. He had stood in it for twenty minutes; he then spent about the same again on the man ahead of him counting out coins, the dog being carried around in a shopping bag, the ticket machine which had been out of order since roughly the previous winter. Not one element of that is amusing. What made it unbearable was his absolute refusal to leave anything out.

Delivery is the other half. He does not crack. In thirty years I have never seen him laugh at his own material, and that flatness is precisely what does the damage. If anything it reads as a form of discipline.

Why I value it has surprisingly little to do with comedy. My relatives are enthusiastic arguers, largely about matters that will never be settled, and the instant he begins one of these monologues the argument evaporates. Even the shyer cousins find their way into it. That, I think, is what a genuinely funny person is for: not the laugh itself, but the fact that a room reorganises itself around them and nobody notices it happening.

what_lifts_it.point: A fronted 'What made it unbearable was' does work band 7 spread over two clauses.
'Canonised', 'he does not crack', 'the argument evaporates' are each chosen for a shade.
It ends by defining what funny people are for, not by praising this particular one.

annotations.span: What made it unbearable was his absolute refusal to leave anything out.
annotations.label: Cleft puts the cause in focus
annotations.why: Front a 'what' clause when one idea has to land harder than the rest.

annotations.span: the argument evaporates
annotations.label: One verb replaces a whole clause
annotations.why: Choose the verb that carries the image and you need fewer words.

annotations.span: He does not crack.
annotations.label: Four words, entirely precise
annotations.why: Short sentences among long ones read as control, not as shortage.

annotations.span: the ticket machine which had been out of order since roughly the previous winter
annotations.label: Past perfect held inside a list
annotations.why: Keeping the tense accurate mid-list is what sustained control looks like.

annotations.span: not the laugh itself, but the fact that a room reorganises itself around them
annotations.label: Closes on a definition
annotations.why: End on a claim about the type, not the person, and the turn rises.

cards.title: what your home town is known for

payload_json.topic: what your home town is known for
questions: Is your home town well known for anything?
Do many visitors come there?
What did you do there at weekends when you were younger?
Is there anything you'd tell people not to bother with?
Would you like to live there again in the future?

teaching.tense_focus: present simple for the place, past simple for weekends, 'would' for the future
teaching.band_move: Give what it's known for, then say whether you agree with the reputation. That clause is the mark.

questions.answer_shape: Name the thing, say how well known it is, then add one detail.
questions.extend_move: Mildly, yes. There's a bridge everybody photographs, which is honestly the whole of it.

common_error.wrong: My town is famous with its bridge.
common_error.right: My town is famous for its bridge.
common_error.why: 'Famous' takes 'for', never 'with'.

questions.answer_shape: Give a rough quantity, say when they come, then who they are.
questions.extend_move: A fair number in summer, hardly anybody the rest of the year.

common_error.wrong: Many tourist come in summer.
common_error.right: A lot of tourists come in summer.
common_error.why: 'Many' and 'a lot of' both need a plural noun.

questions.answer_shape: Past simple, one activity, then where you went to do it.
questions.extend_move: Not much, honestly. We used to sit by the river because there was nowhere else to sit.

common_error.wrong: We are going to the river every Saturday.
common_error.right: We used to go to the river every Saturday.
common_error.why: A repeated past habit takes 'used to'.

questions.answer_shape: Name one thing, give the reason, then soften the judgement.
questions.extend_move: The museum, probably. It's two rooms and one of them is a gift shop.

common_error.wrong: I advise them to don't go there.
common_error.right: I'd tell them not to bother.

questions.probe: What would you send them to instead?

questions.answer_shape: Answer with 'would', attach a condition, then say what would need to change.
questions.extend_move: Possibly later on. I'd need the work to be there, which it currently isn't.

common_error.right: I'd like to live there when I'm older.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to describe my aunt. She is the sister of my father and she has a small bakery in our town.

She gave me a very useful advice when I was twenty years old. At that time I have a problem because I got a job offer and also I got a place in a course, and I don't know what to choose. So I asked everybody, my parents, my friends, my old teacher. Everybody said something different, so after that it was more confusing for me than before.

Then one day I was in her kitchen and I am telling her about this problem again. And she said, take a paper and write the answer that you already choose. Just write it. So I wrote it and it was the course. I wrote it very fast, without thinking.

Then she said, so you are not confused, you only want somebody to say it is okay. And this was true. So I took the course and I never regret it. She is a very practical person and this is why her advice was so useful for me.

what_caps_it.point: 'Advice' is treated as countable, and 'useful' and 'practical' carry every judgement.
'I have a problem' and 'I am telling her' sit inside a past narrative.

model_answers.transcript:
The one who comes to mind is my father's sister, who runs a small bakery in the town I grew up in. She's not somebody I'd have thought of as an adviser, which is probably why it worked.

This was when I was about twenty. I'd been offered a job and I'd also been given a place on a course, and the two of them started within a fortnight of each other. I asked everybody I could think of, and every single one of them had a different opinion, so by the end of that I was considerably less clear than when I started. That went on for the better part of three weeks.

I was sitting in her kitchen going over the whole thing yet again when she stopped me. She pushed a piece of paper across the table and said, write down the one you've already chosen. Not the one you should choose. The one you've already chosen. I wrote 'course' without thinking about it at all, which took roughly two seconds. She didn't even look up while I was writing.

And then she said the thing I still repeat to people: you're not undecided, you just want somebody to tell you it's all right. That was exactly what had been going on. I'd been collecting opinions rather than weighing anything up, because the choice had already been made and I hadn't admitted it. The useful part, in hindsight, wasn't the advice. It was being told what I was actually doing.

model_answers.transcript:
The person I'd point to is my father's sister. She runs a bakery, has never given a lecture in her life, and is the only person whose advice I have ever acted on immediately.

I was twenty and stuck between a job and a place on a course, both of them starting inside a fortnight. In the weeks before that, I had consulted, by my own count, nine separate people. All nine were confident, none of them agreed, and the net effect was that I understood the choice rather less well than before I began. It is a peculiar kind of paralysis, and I would not recommend it to anybody.

She listened to about four minutes of it in her kitchen and then slid a sheet of paper across the table. Write down the one you have already picked, she said. Not the sensible one. The one you have already picked. I wrote it in about two seconds, which was itself the answer.

Then came the line I have been quoting ever since: you are not undecided, you simply want permission. She was entirely right. What I had been doing was canvassing until somebody ratified a decision I had made weeks earlier and could not own. Rarely have I been read that accurately by anybody. And I think the lesson generalises: the most useful people are not the ones who tell you what to do, but the ones who describe what you are doing.

This was about seven years ago. I was on an overnight coach to another city for an interview, and the coach broke down at around midnight. The person I'd choose is somebody I spent five hours with and cannot name, which is precisely why she has lasted.

Seven years ago I was on an overnight coach, travelling to an interview in another city, and somewhere around midnight the thing gave out. We were decanted into a service station forecourt and left there for the best part of four hours, in the cold, with everything shut. I had been asleep and was in no mood for any of it.

She was across the aisle. Sixties, on her way to a hospital appointment first thing, entirely unbothered by the delay. model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a time I explained something difficult. It was to my grandmother and it was about her bank.

Last year her bank closed the branch in her town and they said everything is on the app now. She is eighty-one and she never used a smartphone before. My uncle explained her two times and the bank explained also, but she doesn't understand anything. She was very worried, she thought maybe her money is gone.

So I went to her house on a Sunday. First I show her the app, step by step, this button, then this button. But it was not working. She was more confused than before. Then I stopped and I asked her, what do you think happens with your money. And she said, it is in the building. She thought the money is physically inside the branch, like in a box.

So then I took a paper and I drew it. The bank, the computer, and the money is only a number. After that it was easy, in ten minutes she was fine.

I felt happy but also stupid, because I explained one hour the wrong thing. So this is the time I explained something difficult.

model_answers.transcript:
The occasion I'd pick is explaining online banking to my grandmother, which sounds trivial and absolutely was not.

Her local branch shut about a year ago and the bank moved more or less everything onto an app. She's eighty-one and had never owned a smartphone. By the time I got involved, my uncle had been through it with her twice and somebody at the bank had tried as well, and none of it had landed. What worried me was that she'd started saying she no longer knew where her money was, which is not a small thing to be thinking at eighty-one.

I went round on a Sunday and did exactly what everybody else had done. I opened the app and walked her through it, screen by screen. Twenty minutes in, it was clear this was going nowhere, so I stopped and asked her what she thought actually happened to her money when she paid it in. And she said it stayed in the building.

That was the whole problem. In fairness, it was an obvious thing to have checked. She wasn't confused about the app at all; she was confused about where money lives. So I drew it on the back of an envelope, the branch on one side and a number in a computer on the other. After that the app itself took about ten minutes.

What I took from it is that most failed explanations are answers to the wrong question. If I'd asked first instead of explaining first, I'd have saved us both an hour.

model_answers.transcript:
The episode I'd choose is teaching my grandmother to bank on a phone, which I had assumed would take about twenty minutes.

Her branch closed last year and the bank shifted everything onto an app. She is eighty-one and had never held a smartphone. Two people had already attempted it before me, my uncle and somebody at the counter, and both attempts had sunk without trace. The detail that alarmed me was a remark she made about no longer knowing where her money was, which at eighty-one is not a small sentence.

I went round on the Sunday and proceeded to repeat everybody else's mistake. I opened the application and took her through it screen by screen, patiently and uselessly, for the better part of an hour. Only when I gave up did I think to ask what she believed happened to money once she had handed it over the counter. It stayed in the building, she said. She offered this without a trace of hesitation.

There was the entire problem. The obstacle was never the interface; it was a model of banking formed in about 1960 and never revised since. Two minutes with a pen and an envelope sorted it, and the app followed in ten.

What that taught me has outlasted the banking. Almost every explanation that fails is a well-constructed answer to a question nobody asked. Had I begun by finding out what she already believed, I would have saved us both the hour.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to describe a time when somebody was very kind to me. It happened about four years ago in November.

I was driving back from my cousin's house and my car stopped on a small road. It was nine o'clock in the night and it was very dark and cold. I try to call somebody but there was no signal on my phone. So I was waiting there for forty minutes and nobody stopped, maybe three cars passed but they don't stop.

Then a small van stopped. There was a woman inside, maybe fifty years old. She opened the window and she asked me what happened. I explained her about the car. And then she said, get in, I take you to the garage. The garage was twenty kilometres away in another town. She drove me there and she waited also, because it was closed and we must find the man with the key.

After that I want to give her some money but she refused. She said, somebody did this for me before, fifteen years ago. And then she went away. I was very surprised because she doesn't know me at all. So this is the time I was surprised by somebody's kindness.

what_caps_it.point: 'I try', 'they don't stop' and 'I want to give' all sit inside a past narrative.
'Kind', 'surprised' and 'very dark' carry the whole event between them.
A chain of events joined by 'and' and 'so', with the point never actually made.

annotations.why: Both verbs in one sentence must match: 'passed' and 'didn't stop'.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The occasion I'd choose happened about four years ago, in November, on a completely unremarkable stretch of road.

I'd been at my cousin's and I was driving home when the car simply died. This was somewhere around nine in the evening, in the middle of nowhere, and it turned out there was no signal at all where I'd stopped. I stood at the side of the road for the best part of forty minutes. Three or four cars went past without slowing down, which I honestly don't blame them for, and it was getting properly cold by then. I remember thinking I'd have to walk it.

Then a small van pulled up. The driver was a woman in her fifties, and she wound the window down and asked what had happened. Once I'd explained, she just said get in. She drove me twenty kilometres to a garage in the next town, and when it turned out to be shut she waited with me until we'd tracked somebody down. That took another hour, easily.

The part that surprised me was the end of it. I tried to give her something for the petrol and she wouldn't hear of it. All she said was that somebody had done the same for her about fifteen years earlier, and then she drove off before I could ask her anything else at all. I've thought about that a great deal since. It wasn't really kindness towards me at all; it was more like a debt being passed along, and I'm the one holding it now.

'Simply died', 'wouldn't hear of it' and 'a debt being passed along' do the evaluating.
The surprise is held back and then explained, so the fourth bullet has somewhere to go.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The occasion I'd pick took place about four years ago on a November evening, on a road with nothing on it in either direction.

I was driving back from my cousin's when the car gave up entirely. Nine o'clock, pitch dark, and of course no signal wherever it was that I had stopped. I stood on the verge for the best part of forty minutes. Several cars came past and not one of them slowed, which in fairness is probably what I would have done myself. It is a long forty minutes when nothing is coming.

Then a small van pulled in. A woman in her fifties, window down, asking what the trouble was. Having heard about thirty seconds of it she told me to get in, drove me twenty kilometres to a garage in the next town, found it shut, and then waited with me for another hour while we located somebody with a key.

What has stayed with me is not the lift. It is what she said when I tried to press some money on her for the fuel. She would not take a penny, and remarked, almost in passing, that somebody had done exactly this for her fifteen years earlier. That reframed the whole evening. It had very little to do with me at all; I had simply been handed something that was already in circulation, and at some point I am expected to pass it on.

annotations.why: One well-chosen image replaces a paragraph of explaining.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about something I do with my family every week. Every Sunday morning we go to the market together.

We are doing this since four years. It started when my father stopped working, because before that he is always busy at the weekend also. Now he have more free time. So every Sunday we wake up early, maybe seven o'clock, and me and my father and my younger brother we walk to the market. It takes twenty minutes to walk there.

At the market we buy the vegetables and the fruit for the week. My father always want to go to the same man because he says his tomatoes are better. My brother says it is the same tomatoes everywhere. So they argue every week about this, it is a joke in our family now. After that we go to a small cafe near there and we drink coffee and we sit maybe one hour.

I like it very much because in the week we don't talk really. We only talk about things like who is taking the car. But on Sunday we talk about normal things. So this is the thing I do with my family regularly.

what_caps_it.point: Third-person -s is dropped repeatedly, and 'since four years' needs a present perfect.
'Like it very much', 'better' and 'normal things' are the whole evaluative range.
'So' opens four sentences, and the turn finishes by reading the card back.

annotations.label: Gives one recurring detail
annotations.why: Keep this. A repeated detail is what proves a routine is real.

annotations.span: We are doing this since four years.
annotations.label: Wrong tense and wrong preposition
annotations.why: Say 'We've been doing it for about four years'.

annotations.span: Now he have more free time.
annotations.label: Third-person -s dropped
annotations.why: 'He has more free time'. This is the single most-noticed slip there is.

annotations.span: My father always want to go to the same man
annotations.label: The -s goes missing again
annotations.why: 'My father always wants to go'. Habitual present needs the ending.

annotations.span: in the week we don't talk really
annotations.label: Adverb misplaced, meaning blurred
annotations.why: Say 'during the week we don't really talk'.

annotations.label: Closes on the card's wording
annotations.why: End on what the routine gives you that the rest of the week doesn't.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The thing I'd describe is a walk to the market that the three of us do every Sunday morning. It's my father, my younger brother and me, and we've been doing it for about four years now.

It started when my father retired. Before that he worked most weekends, so Sunday morning was the first slot in the week that was genuinely free, and I think he wanted something in it. We leave at about seven, which is unreasonable, and walk for twenty minutes or so to the market on the far side of town. None of us has ever suggested going later.

The routine barely varies, which is half the point. We buy the vegetables for the week, my father insists on one particular stall because he maintains the tomatoes there are better, and my brother says every week that tomatoes are tomatoes. They've been having that argument for four years and neither of them has moved an inch. Then we sit in the same café for an hour, in the same three chairs, and nobody's in any hurry about any of it.

What I get out of it isn't really the market. During the week the three of us only ever talk about arrangements: who needs the car, who's collecting what. Sunday is the one stretch where nothing has to be decided. I'd say that's what a routine is actually for. It isn't the activity at all, it's the fact that the time is already booked and nobody has to propose it.

what_lifts_it.point: Present perfect continuous for the duration, and a present simple that never slips.
'Barely varies', 'insists on' and 'hasn't moved an inch' replace 'always' and 'very good'.
The last paragraph explains the routine instead of describing yet more of it.

annotations.label: Names everybody in one clause
annotations.why: Get the cast in early and you never have to stop to introduce anyone.

annotations.span: we've been doing it for about four years now
annotations.label: Present perfect continuous for duration
annotations.why: Use it whenever a habit began in the past and is still running.

annotations.span: The routine barely varies, which is half the point.
annotations.label: Evaluates while it describes
annotations.why: One evaluative verb saves you a whole sentence of explanation.

annotations.span: They've been having that argument for four years and neither of them has moved an inch.
annotations.label: Duration plus a negative subject
annotations.why: 'Neither of them has' takes a singular verb, and examiners listen for it.

annotations.span: What I get out of it isn't really the market.
annotations.label: Signposts the explain bullet
annotations.why: Announce it and the bullet that carries most of the band gets covered.

annotations.span: nobody's in any hurry
annotations.label: Spoken chunk, not a formal phrase
annotations.why: This is what people say; 'we relax together' is what textbooks say.

annotations.span: I'd say that's what a routine is actually for.
annotations.label: Generalises before the close
annotations.why: Move from your household to routines in general and the answer gains altitude.

annotations.span: who needs the car, who's collecting what
annotations.label: Two groups on one contour
annotations.why: Parallel phrases share a rhythm; break it and the pattern disappears.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The routine I'd pick is a Sunday-morning walk to the market, done by three of us, and it has been running for roughly four years.

It began, as these things do, when my father retired. Until then he had worked most weekends, so Sunday was the first genuinely unclaimed morning he'd had in decades, and I suspect he wanted it occupied by something. We set off around seven, which nobody has ever formally agreed to, and walk twenty minutes across town in whatever weather happens to be available.

What makes it work is that nothing about it changes. We buy the week's vegetables; my father will not be moved from one particular stall on the grounds that its tomatoes are superior; my brother observes, weekly, that a tomato is a tomato. Four years of this and neither has conceded a millimetre. Neither of them ever will, either. Afterwards there is an hour in the same café, in the same three chairs, and nobody hurries anybody about anything.

The market, though, is not the point. Our weekday conversation consists almost entirely of logistics, who needs the car and who is collecting whom, and Sunday is the only stretch in which nothing at all has to be settled. That, I have come to think, is what a shared routine really provides. Not the activity, but a block of time that has already been agreed, so that nobody ever has to be the one who suggests it.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Will not be moved' as habitual refusal, and 'whom' used where it genuinely belongs.
'Unclaimed', 'conceded a millimetre' and 'observes, weekly' each carry judgement precisely.
The final sentence defines what routines are for rather than restating this one.

annotations.span: my father will not be moved from one particular stall
annotations.label: 'Will' for habitual insistence
annotations.why: 'Will not' about a habit means refuses every time; it is not a future.

annotations.span: who needs the car and who is collecting whom
annotations.label: 'Whom' in its correct slot
annotations.why: Use it only where it belongs; used wrongly it costs more than it gains.

annotations.span: neither has conceded a millimetre
annotations.label: Precise exaggeration, correctly formed
annotations.why: 'Neither has' plus a tiny unit does the humour and the grammar at once.

annotations.span: the first genuinely unclaimed morning
annotations.label: One adjective replaces a clause
annotations.why: Reach for the adjective that carries the whole idea, then move on.

annotations.span: Not the activity, but a block of time that has already been agreed
annotations.label: Ends on a definition
annotations.why: Generalise at the very end and it stops being only your household.

annotations.span: my brother observes, weekly, that a tomato is a tomato
annotations.label: The aside slows and drops
annotations.why: A parenthesis delivered flatter than the sentence around it reads as dry.
